\tag{C.7}\]
We make the assumption that interference respects some mapping between individuals - a mapping given by a graph adjacency matrix \(\Psi\). In Figure C.6, based on their relationships with one another, Person 1’s measures are connected with Person 2’s, and neither are connected with Person 3’s.
\[
\Psi = \begin{bmatrix}
0,& 1,& 0 \\
1,& 0,& 0 \\
0,& 0,& 0 \\
\end{bmatrix}
\]


Homogeneity I: Homogenous network interference
We assume that the exposure mapping for each variable in the structural model is separable. i.e. We define \(g_{A_i}\), \(h_{Y_i}\), and \(g_{Y_i}\) as component functions for \(A_i\) with respect to \(\mathbf{L}\), for \(Y_i\) with respect to \(\mathbf{A}\), and for \(Y_i\) with respect to \(\mathbf{L}\). The assumption of separability allows us to write the model as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_1 &= f_{L_1}(U_{L_1}) \\
L_2 &= f_{L_2}(U_{L_2}) \\
L_3 &= f_{L_3}(U_{L_3} ) \\
A_1 &= f_{A_1}(U_{A_1}, L_1, g_{A_1}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_1)) \\
A_2 &= f_{A_2}(U_{A_2}, L_2, g_{A_2}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_2)) \\
A_3 &= f_{A_3}(U_{A_3}, L_3, g_{A_3}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_3)) \\
Y_1 &= f_{Y_1}(U_{Y_1}, L_1, A_1, g_{Y_1}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_1), h_{Y_1}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_1)) \\
Y_2 &= f_{Y_2}(U_{Y_2}, L_2, A_2, g_{Y_2}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_2), h_{Y_2}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_2)) \\
Y_3 &= f_{Y_3}(U_{Y_3}, L_3,A_3,  g_{Y_2}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_3), h_{Y_2}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_3)) \\
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\Psi_i\) is the \(i^{th}\) row of matrix \(\Psi\).
We assume that the value of a component function is invariant to its position in the network. This allows us to drop the person subscript on the network exposure mappings.
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_1 &= f_{L_1}(U_{L_1}) \\
L_2 &= f_{L_2}(U_{L_2}) \\
L_3 &= f_{L_3}(U_{L_3} ) \\
A_1 &= f_{A_1}(U_{A_1}, L_1, g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_1)) \\
A_2 &= f_{A_2}(U_{A_2}, L_2, g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_2)) \\
A_3 &= f_{A_3}(U_{A_3}, L_3, g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_3)) \\
Y_1 &= f_{Y_1}(U_{Y_1}, L_1, A_1, g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_1), h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_1)) \\
Y_2 &= f_{Y_2}(U_{Y_2}, L_2, A_2, g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_2), h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_2)) \\
Y_3 &= f_{Y_3}(U_{Y_3}, L_3,A_3,  g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_3), h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_3)) \\
\end{aligned}
\]
We also assume its bounded, meaning
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i) &\in \{0, 1\} \\
g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i) &\in \{0, 1\} \\
h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_i) &\in \{0, 1\} \\
\end{aligned}
\]


Homogeneity II: Identical distributions
We assume that the structural equations that produce individual measures are identical across individuals. Hence, we can drop the person subscript from the structural equations.
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_1 &= f_{L}(U_{L_1}) \\
L_2 &= f_{L}(U_{L_2}) \\
L_3 &= f_{L}(U_{L_3} ) \\
A_1 &= f_{A}(U_{A_1}, L_1, g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_1)) \\
A_2 &= f_{A}(U_{A_2}, L_2, g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_2)) \\
A_3 &= f_{A}(U_{A_3}, L_3, g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_3)) \\
Y_1 &= f_{Y}(U_{Y_1}, L_1, A_1, g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_1), h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_1)) \\
Y_2 &= f_{Y}(U_{Y_2}, L_2, A_2, g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_2), h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_2)) \\
Y_3 &= f_{Y}(U_{Y_3}, L_3,A_3,  g_{Y}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_3), h_{Y}(\mathbf{A}, \Psi_3)) \\
\end{aligned}
\]



C.2.2 Structural equations

Observed data model
Figure C.7 and Equation C.8 show the resulting NPSEM and DAG for our data. Because of the assumption of identical distributions, we can represent the model using three equations rather than nine. We retain the person subscript on the random variables in Equation C.8 and we keep all nine nodes in the DAG on Figure C.7 and add six additional nodes to represent network exposure values with respect to \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{L}\).
We draw the DAG like this to clarify that though our model is for one person, it represents a part of a system that relates all the people in the sample with each other. Our original purpose, after all, was to infer something about the sample, not any one individual in it.


Code
make_dag("homogenous_interference")            |> 
  plot_swig(node_radius = 0.2) + 
  scale_fill_mpxnyc(option = "light") +
  scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("covariate" = "black")) +
  theme_mpxnyc_blank()








Figure C.7: Causal DAG with homogenous structure





We can re-write the structural equation model like this:
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_i &= f_{L}( U_{L_i} ) \\
A_i &= f_{A}( U_{A_i}, L_i, g_{A}(\textbf{L}, \Psi_i) ) \\
Y_i &= f_{Y}( U_{Y_i},  L_i,  g_{Y}(\textbf{L}, \Psi_i),   A_i,  h_{Y}( \textbf{A}, \Psi_i ) ) \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.8}\]


Counterfactual data model
We define counterfactual outcomes \(Y_1^{(a_1, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_1})}\), \(Y_2^{(a_2, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_2})}\), and \(Y_3^{(a_3, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_3})}\), which represent the level of job opportunities, Persons 1, 2, and 3, would have if we set their dress to level \(a_1\), \(a_2\), and \(a_3\), respectively. Then the model for counterfactual variable is given by Equation C.9. It is represented using a SWIG in Figure C.8.
Note that because of the assumption of network interference, the counterfactual outcome for Person 1 is a function of Person 2’s treatment value and vice versa. The counterfactual outcome for Person 3, on the other hand, is a function of Person 3’s treatment (\(a_3\)) alone. This is because \(\mathscr{N}_1 = \{2\}\), \(\mathscr{N}_2 = \{1\}\), and \(\mathscr{N}_3 = \{\}\), according to Example 2.
To ensure that counterfactual outcomes are well-defined for all experimental units, we make the assumption of positivity:
\[
0 < P[A_i = a_i,  h_Y (\mathbf{A}, \Psi_i) =  h_Y(\mathbf{a}, \Psi_i)| L_i,g_{A}(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i) ] < 1
\] for all \(\mathbf{a} \in \{0,1\}^n\)


Code
make_swig("homogenous_interference")      |> 
  plot_swig(node_radius = 0.2, nudge_intervention_labels = 0.16) + 
  scale_fill_mpxnyc(option = "light") +
  scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("covariate" = "black", "intervention" = "black")) + 
  theme_mpxnyc_blank()








Figure C.8: SWIG with homogenous





\[
\begin{aligned}
L_i &= f_{L}(  U_{L_i}  ) \\
A_i &= f_{A}( U_{A_i}, L_i, g_{A}(\textbf{L}, \Psi_i) ) \\
Y_i^{(a_i,\textbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} )} &= f_{Y}(U_{Y_i}, L_i,  a_i,  g_{Y}(\textbf{L}, \Psi_i),      h_{Y}(\textbf{a}, \Psi_i)         ) \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.9}\]



C.2.3 Estimands
We are interested in whether on average, changing someone’s dress would change their level of job offers. To determine the answer, we will compare the average counterfactual outcome of job opportunities if everyone were forced to wear formal dress to the average counterfactual outcome of job opportunities if everyone wore non-formal dress. i.e. We will make the following comparison:
\[
ATE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[Y_i^{(a = 1, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} = \textbf{ 1})} - Y_i^{(a = 0, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} = \textbf{ 0})}]
\] It is possible to decompose this average causal effect into a portion attributable to direct (within individual) causal pathways. This tells us, on average, to what extent one’s own dress affects one own’s job opportunities.
\[
ADE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[Y_i^{(a = 1, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} = \textbf{ 0})} - Y_i^{(a = 0, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} = \textbf{ 0})}]
\]
We can calculate the portion of the average total effect attributable to spillover (cross-individual) causal pathways. This tells us, on average, to what extent one’s spouse’s dress affects one’s job opportunities.
\[
ASE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[Y_i^{(a = 1, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} = \textbf{ 1})} - Y_i^{(a = 1, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i} = \textbf{ 0})}]
\]


C.2.4 Identification
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y_i^{(a_i, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i})} ]
&=  E[E[Y_i^{(a_i, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i})} | \mathbf{L}]]   \\
&=  E[E[Y_i^{(a_i, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i})}                                  | L_i , g_Y(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i)] ] \\
&=  E[E[f_{Y}(U_{Y_i}, L_i,  a_i, g_{Y}(\textbf{L}, \Psi_i),  h_{Y}(\textbf{a}, \Psi_i))   | L_i , g_Y(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i)] ] \\
&=  E[E[f_{Y}(...)                                                               | L_i , g_Y(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i), A_i = a_i, h_Y(\textbf{A}, \Psi_i) = h_Y(\textbf{a}, \Psi_i)]] \\
&=  E[E[Y_i                                                                      | L_i , g_Y(\mathbf{L}, \Psi_i), A_i = a_i, h_Y(\textbf{A}, \Psi_i) = h_Y(\textbf{a}, \Psi_i)]] \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In the first line we use the law of iterated expectations. In the second line, we use the separability of the structural equation for \(Y_i^{(a_i, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i})}\). In the third line we replace substitute for the structural equation. In the fourth line, we use the fact that in the counterfactual model, \(\mathbf{A}\) is independent of \(f_{Y}(...)\) conditional on \(\mathbf{L}\). In the final line we use the fact that structural equation for \(Y_i^{(a_i, \mathbf{a}_{\mathscr{N}_i})}\) in the counterfactual data NPSEM-IE is identical to the structural equation for \(Y_i\) in the observed data NPSEM-IE.


C.2.5 Notes

We have turned a non-iid situation into a form that is tractible using approaches that usually require IID.
The reason this works is that the assumption of IID is stronger than necessary in most applications. For regression modesl, we require conditional independence between observation, not independence. We simply take up the room between the independence and conditional independence assumptions and tame it using graphs.
This is great if we know the entire graph - we can accurately calculate network exposure values for each observation in order to estimate functionals of the structural equations.
But if we only have a random sample of the nodes in a network, which would be the most optimistic scenario in most applications, the average degree will be lower in the sampled network than in the entire network. To the extent network exposure values are correlated, they will be biased, leading to biased estimates of the structural equations.
One approach to bridge this situation would be to build into models, both the mechanism generating the network (the graph generators), and the mechanism for censoring the nodes, to generate estimates that account for those.
Another approach might be to solicit informatio about the network from the nodes themselves, and calculate network exposure values using measures taken exclusively on each given observation. The measurement error would be significant, and would likely need to be incorporated into the model as well.
For linear regression models, for instance, we need only know the mean degree of the graph and each observation’s network exposure values to identify the coefficients of a model which exhibits homogenous network interference.
In the next section we side-step these issues by focusing on bipartite networks of people and places where we have a full listing of places and a possibly censored listing of people. In this setting, it is possible to accurately observe the network exposure values of the person nodes included in the sample since these values are a function of values taken on place nodes, which are fully observed.

plot_icon(icon_name = "droplets", color = "dark_purple", shape = 0)

title: C - SSNAC III: Causality
text:
C.3 Social-spatial networks
In this section, we provide an overview of a new approach to causal inference — causal social-spatial network analysis. Whereas in causal social network analysis it is complicated to imagine the relationships between the sample and the universe (since the sample units are interrelated), in this approach we keep the simplicity of random sampling while engaging the insights possible to gain from networked analysis.






Learning goals





After this section, you will be equipped to:

Write an NPSEM of the whole sample for a model that includes network generators

Draw the corresponding DANG

Apply the assumption of homogeneous network interference to an NPSEM that includes network generators










Example 3: Vaccination



You are a public health officer at the department of health in Exampleville and are planning to conduct and assess a three-week flu vaccination campaign. None of the townspeople have been vaccinated against flu. There is a population of six residents in the city, and they each live in one of three neighborhoods. In addition, residents visit their friends’ homes in other neighborhoods.
At time 0, Person 1 lives in Neighborhood A and visits Neighborhood B. Person 2 lives in Neighborhood B, but visits Neighborhoods A and B. Person 3 lives in Neighborhood C and visits Neighborhood B. Persons 5 and 6 live in Neighborhood C and do not visit any other neighborhoods. At the beginning of each week, before any public-health activities, each resident of Exampleville has the opportunity to change the neighborhoods they live in and visit.
The city of Exampleville has a structured approach to vaccination campaigns. At the beginning of each week, each neighborhood gets a risk rating based on the prevalence of vaccination among its residents and visitors. Based on that rating, each neighborhood decides whether to conduct a local vaccination drive.
Vaccination drives are conducted in the same way regardless of neighborhood — visitors and residents are offered immediate vaccination at a nearby mobile van through a pop-up message on the local dating app. Not everyone will receive the messages because some will not open the app during the campaign period. Those who do will have the choice of getting vaccinated or not. Each person can only get vaccinated once.








 Toolkit C: Causal reasoning under random bipartite network interference



In this section of the appendix, we extend the NFFRCISTG model described in Section C.2 by allowing for the inclusion of two classes of observational unit — people and places — and by allowing the relationships between people and places to be randomly generated by the causal model. We name this the Bipartite Random Network FFRCISTG model (BRNFFRCISTG). It is a causal model that includes one or more graph generators — structural equations that model the network edges as random variables.
Before outlining the BRNFFRCISTG, we introduce new tools to mirror the shift we advocate from conceiving of statistical inference as the task of inferring something about a probability distribution using a growing number of realizations, to thinking about it as the task of inferring something about the distribution using one growing realization of the model. We introduce the causal Directed Acyclic Network Graph (DANG) and the Single World Intervention Network Graph (SWING).






DANGs





DANGs encode the structure of the causal process within individuals separately from the structure of the causal process across individuals. The former is termed the structural part of the DANG and the latter the relational part. The relational part shows which pairs of observational units influence each other. For instance, in Figure C.9 we see that individuals 1 and 2 are related.
The structural part is a DAG of vector-valued variables whose length equals the number of observational units in the sample. It has the standard interpretation under d-separation rules: it gives the conditional independencies across these vector-valued random variables. For instance, below is a DANG of the model we developed for Example 2.
The structural part is a DAG of vector-valued variables \(\mathbf{L}\), \(\mathbf{A}\), and \(\mathbf{Y}\) of length equal to the number of people in the sample. It shows the relationship between units 1 and 2 separately from the causal structure linking employment, dress, and job opportunities.


Code
structural <- example_dang_1_structural() |>
                    plot_swig(node_radius = 0.2) +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = "black") +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank()+
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Structural Part") 

relational <- example_dang_1_relational() |>
                    plot_swig(0, 0, node_radius = 0.2)  +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(name = "Entity type", option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = "black") +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank() +
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Relational Part") 

cowplot::plot_grid(structural, relational, ncol = 1)








Figure C.9: Causal DANG














Mixed DANGs





DANGs not only allow for compact notation in causal systems characterized by interference; they can describe causal systems that involve more than one kind of observational unit. We focus on systems that involve persons as one unit type and places as the other. Figure C.10 shows a DANG for the first week of the campaign mentioned in Example 2. Let () be the decision to conduct a vaccination campaign or not in each of the three places. () indicates whether each of the six people received a vaccination-campaign message. () indicates whether each of the people got vaccinated.


Code
structural  <- example_dang_2_structural() |>
                    plot_swig(node_radius = 0.15) +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(name = "Entity type", option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("Community" = "black", "Individual" = "black", "intervention" = "black")) +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank() +
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Structural Part")


relational  <- example_dang_2_relational() |>
                    plot_swig(node_radius = 0.2, node_margin = 0)  +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(name = "Entity type", option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("Community" = "black", "Individual" = "black", "intervention" = "black")) +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank() +
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Relational Part") 

figure   <- cowplot::plot_grid(structural, relational, ncol=1, rel_heights = c(3,3))



legend_pre  <- relational + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "right")

legend      <- cowplot::get_legend(legend_pre) 
 
   
cowplot::plot_grid(figure, legend, nrow = 1, rel_widths = c(4,1))








Figure C.10: Causal DANG for Week 1 in Example 3














SWINGs





We introduce the Single World Intervention Network Graph (SWING) — an extension of the SWIG that allows for the representation of the counterfactual outcomes of interventions in complex causal systems.


Code
structural  <- example_swing_structural() |>
                    plot_swig(node_radius = 0.15) +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("Community" = "black", "Individual" = "black", "intervention" = "black")) +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank() +
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Structural Part") 


relational  <- example_swing_relational() |>
                    plot_swig(node_radius = 0.2, node_margin = 0)  +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(name = "Entity type", option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("Community" = "black", "Individual" = "black", "intervention" = "black")) +
                    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "right") +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank() +
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Relational Part")


legend_pre  <- relational +
                    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "right")
legend      <- cowplot::get_legend(legend_pre) 



figure   <- cowplot::plot_grid(structural, relational, ncol=1, rel_heights = c(3,3))

cowplot::plot_grid(figure, legend, nrow = 1, rel_widths = c(4,1))








Figure C.11: SWING for Week 1 in Example 3





Like the DANG, the SWING has two parts: a structural part and a relational part.
The SWING also represents vector-valued random variables (rather than scalars) as nodes. Like the SWIG, the SWING splits the nodes that are to be intervened upon by the experimenter. Figure C.11 shows the counterfactual distribution of the variables in the model under an intervention setting () to the value ().









Random graphs





Random graphs bring probability into the network itself. Instead of assuming we know which edges exist, we treat them as random variables. In Example 3, for instance, every week the townspeople possibly change their community of residence and/or the communities they visit. Random graphs allow us to model a time-varying pattern of interference, or even different patterns of interference for different variables.









Bipartite graphs





A bipartite graph is one where nodes are divided into two disjoint sets and edges connect only across sets. In random-interference problems, it is often useful to model people on one side and places or events on the other. An edge then represents a person’s affiliation with a place, and interference arises because multiple people may be connected through the same location. This structure allows us to represent exposures that are not purely person-to-person, but mediated by shared environments.


Code
 example_dang_2_relational() |>
                    plot_swig(node_radius = 0.2, node_margin = 0)  +
                    scale_fill_mpxnyc(name = "Entity type", option = "light") +
                    scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("Community" = "black", "Individual" = "black", "intervention" = "black")) +
                    theme_mpxnyc_blank() +
                    ggplot2::ggtitle("Bipartite Graph") 








Figure C.12: Example of bipartite graph














Homogeneous random network interference





We assume that homogeneous interference holds, given a set of random draws from the random-graph models included. This mirrors the homogeneous-interference assumption from the fixed-network setting, but now exposures vary both with treatment assignments and with the random realization of the network.









Formal definitions






Definition C.27 (Graph generator) An \(n \times n\) array of structural equations which collectively model the edges of a random graph.
An \(n \times n\) function \([f_{\psi_{ij}}]_{i,j \in \mathcal N}\) whose entries \(\psi(i,j)\) are each a deterministic symmetric function of the other variables in the model along with an error term.
\[
\psi(i,j) = f_{\psi_{ij}}(\mathbf{Pa}(\psi(i,j)), U_{\psi_{ij}})
\]
such that
\[
U_{\psi_{ij}} = U_{\psi_{ji}} \text{ and } f_{\psi_{ij}} = f_{\psi_{ji}}
\]


Definition C.28 (NPSEM-NE) An NPSEM with networked errors is an NPSEM which includes random graph generators among the structural equations. Error terms are correlated within each graph generator but independent across graph generators, between structural equations and graph generators, and between structural equations.


Definition C.29 (Homogenous random network interference) An exposure mapping exhibits homogeneous random network interference with respect to a random graph set \(\{\psi_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}\) if it is separable and all its component functions are network exposure mappings. An NPSEM exhibiits homogenous random network interference if all its exposure mappings exhibit homogenous randomn network interference.


Definition C.30 (RNFFRCISTG) A random network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (RNFFRCISTG) model is a causal model defined on a random graph NPSEM-NE which satisfies the (1) no spillover, (2) homogenous random network interference with respect to random graph set \(\mathcal H \subset \mathbf V\), and (3) identical distributions assumptions.


Definition C.31 (Bipartite NPSEM-IE) A random bipartite graph NPSEM-IE is a random graph NPSEM which whose generators produce bipartite graphs on the same partitioning of \(\mathbf V\).


Definition C.32 (BRNFFRCISTG model) A bipartite random network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (BRNFFRCISTG) model is a causal model defined on a bipartite random graph NPSEM-IE which satisfies the (1) no spillover, (2) homogenous random network interference, and (3) identical distributions assumptions.







C.3.1 Assumptions

Independence assumptions
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Structural} \\
&  \mathbf M_{0}                  & &= f_{\mathbf M_0}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf M_{0}})              \\
&  \mathbf V_{0}                  & &= f_{\mathbf V_0}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf V_{0}})               \\
&  \mathbf R_{s}                   & &= f_{\mathbf R}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf R_{s}}, \mathbf{V}_{s-1}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1}) \\
&  \mathbf T_{s}                   & &= f_{\mathbf T}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf T_{s}}, \mathbf R_{s})                                 \\
&  \mathbf M_{s}                  & &=     f_{\mathbf M} (\mathbf U_{\mathbf M_{s}} , \mathbf V_{s-1,i},   \mathbf M_{s-1}, \mathbf{T}_{s}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s})       \\
&  \mathbf V_{s}                  & &=     f_{\mathbf V}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf V_{s}}, \mathbf M_{s}, \mathbf V_{s-1})                                                \\
\text{Relational} \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{0}   & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}) \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{s}   & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{s}}, \mathbf{V}_{s-1}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1})  \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.10}\]


Homogeneity assumptions

Separability
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Structural} \\
&  \mathbf M_{0}      & &= f_{\mathbf M_0}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf M_{0}})              \\
&  \mathbf V_{0}      & &= f_{\mathbf V_0}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf V_{0}})               \\
&  \mathbf R_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf R}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf R_{s}}, \mathbf g_{\mathbf R} (\mathbf V_{s-1},    \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1})) \\
&  \mathbf T_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf T}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf T_{s}}, \mathbf R_{s})                                 \\
&  \mathbf M_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf M}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf M_{s}}, \mathbf V_{s-1,i},   \mathbf M_{s-1}, g_{\mathbf M} (\mathbf{T}_{s}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s})  )     \\
&  \mathbf V_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf V}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf V_{s}}, \mathbf M_{s},       \mathbf V_{s-1})                                                \\
\text{Relational} \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{0}  & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}) \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{s}  & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{s}}, \mathbf{V}_{s-1}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1})  \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.11}\]


Bipartite
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Structural: People} \\
&  \mathbf M_{0}      & &= f_{\mathbf M_0}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf M_{0}})              \\
&  \mathbf V_{0}      & &= f_{\mathbf V_0}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf V_{0}})               \\
&  \mathbf M_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf M}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf M_{s}}, \mathbf V_{s-1,i},   \mathbf M_{s-1}, g_{\mathbf M} (\mathbf{T}_{s}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s})  )     \\
&  \mathbf V_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf V}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf V_{s}}, \mathbf M_{s},       \mathbf V_{s-1})  \\
\text{Structural: Places} \\
&  \mathbf R_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf R}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf R_{s}}, \mathbf g_{\mathbf R} (\mathbf V_{s-1},    \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1})) \\
&  \mathbf T_{s}      & &= f_{\mathbf T}  (\mathbf U_{\mathbf T_{s}}, \mathbf R_{s})  \\                                              \\
\text{Relational} \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{0}  & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}) \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{s}  & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{s}}, \mathbf{V}_{s-1}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1})  \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.12}\]


Identical distributions
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Structural: People} \\
&   M_{0i}      & &= f_{ M_0}( U_{ M_{0}})              \\
&   V_{0i}      & &= f_{ V_0}( U_{ V_{0}})               \\
&   M_{si}      & &= f_{ M}  ( U_{ M_{s}},  V_{s-1,i},    M_{s-1, i}, g_{\mathbf M} (\mathbf{T}_{s}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{si})  )     \\
&   V_{si}      & &= f_{ V}  ( U_{ V_{s}},  M_{s},        V_{s-1})  \\
\text{Structural: Places} \\
&   R_{sj}      & &= f_{ R}  ( U_{ R_{s}},  g_{ R} (\mathbf V_{s-1},    \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1, j})) \\
&   T_{sj}      & &= f_{ T}  ( U_{ T_{s}},  R_{s})  \\                                              \\
\text{Relational} \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{0}  & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{0}}) \\
&  \mathbf{\Psi}_{s}  & &= f_{\mathbf{\Psi}}(\mathbf U_{\mathbf{\Psi}_{s}}, \mathbf{V}_{s-1}, \mathbf{\Psi}_{s-1})  \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.13}\]
Under the SSNAC framework, we make the assumption of no spillover: contemporaneous measurements on observational units of a given entity type are independent of each other given all prior measures. The time-ordering of the measurements is given by the structural part of the causal DANG. We further make the assumption of network interference - that interference respects the mapping given by the relational part of a causal DANG. i.e. The exposure mapping for each equation in the structural equation model is loyal to the graph that encodes the relational part of the SWING.



Homogeneity assumptions
We make the relational homogeneity assumption which holds that the exposure mappings for variables in the NPSEM are separable and positionally invariant. The structural homogeneity assumption holds that the structural equations that produce each observational unit’s measures are identical across observational units of the same entity type. Finally, we make the boundedness assumption – all the exposure mappings in the NPSEM take values from a finite set. In applications with repeated measures, if the structure of the causal DANG allows, the SSNAC framework allows for the assumption of time homogeneity: the structural equations are identical across time. We apply this assumption in Example 3 below.



C.3.2 Structural equations

Observed data model
The causal DANG shown in Figure C.13 represents the three week campaign mentioned in Example 3. Let \(\mathbf{T}_s\) be a \(3\times1\) vector whose entries \(T_{sj}\) are 1 if Neighborhood \(j\) is to be vaccinated at time \(s\) and \(0\) otherwise. \(\mathbf{M}_s\) is a \(5\times1\) vector whose entries \(M_{si}\) indicate whether the \(i^{\text{th}}\) person received a campaign message at time \(s\) or not. \(\mathbf{V}_s\) is a \(5\times1\) vector whose entries \(V_{si}\) show whether participant \(i\) is vaccinated or not at time \(s\). Finally, \(\mathbf{R}_s\) is a \(3\times1\) vector whose entries \(R_{si}\) shows the risk rating of neighborhood \(j\) at the beginning of time \(s\). Equation C.14 specifies this model for Person \(i\) and Neighborhood \(j\) at time \(s\):

According to Equation C.14, \(R_{sj}\), the risk rating for Neighborhood \(j\) at time \(s\), is a function of \(\mathbf{V}_{s-1}\), the vaccination status of every individual at time \(s-1\). \(T_{sj}\) - an indicator for whether or not Neighborhood \(j\) conducted a campaign at time \(s\), is a function of the risk rating for Neighborhood \(j\) at time \(s\).
\(M_{si}\), which indicates whether or not an Person \(i\) received a campaign message at time \(s\), is a function of whether or not person \(i\) was vaccinated at time \(s-1\), whether they received a campaign message at time \(s-1\), and whether or not one of the neighborhoods they live in or visit conducted a campaign at time \(s\). The vaccination status of individual \(i\) at time \(s\) is a function of whether or not they received a campaign message at time \(s\) and whether or not they were vaccinated at time \(s-1\).


Counterfactual data model
Say we want to understand the impact of a vaccination campaign conducted over three weeks on vaccination status. This would be done by setting \(\mathbf{T}_1\) to \(\mathbf{t}_1\), \(\mathbf{T}_2\) to \(\mathbf{t}_2\), and \(\mathbf{T}_3\) to \(\mathbf{t}_3\) and noting the resulting counterfactual vaccination status at the end of week 1 (\(\mathbf{V}_1^{(\mathbf{t}_1)}\)), week 2 (\(\mathbf{V}_1^{(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2)}\)), and week 3 (\(\mathbf{V}_1^{(\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_2, \mathbf{t}_3)}\)). V_{si}^{(\bar{\mathbf t})} &=  f_{V}(U_{V_{si}}, M_{si}^{(\bar{\mathbf t})}, V_{s-1,k}^{(\bar{\mathbf t})}) \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.15}\]



C.3.3 Estimands
We are interested in vaccine coverage throughout the three week campaign. For a given week \(s\), this is the sum of the vaccine status outcome \(\mathbf{V}\) across individuals.
\[
E[\sum_{i=1}^5 V_{si}^{(\bar{\mathbf t})}]
\]


C.3.4 Identification
Because individual vaccination status is both a confounder and a mediator of the relationship between neighborhood intervention status and vaccination status, we cannot identify our estimands using conditional expectations of the observed data. We must use a marginal structural model.
We can estimate the outcome of interest using the inverse probability of treatment weights, noting that the treatment in this case is the network exposure value \(g(t_{\bar{s},N_i})\) for \(\mathbf{T}\).
\[
V_{si}^{(\bar{\mathbf{t}})} =  \frac{V_{si} \mathbf{1}_{x = g(t_{\bar{s},N_i}) }(g(T_{\bar{s},N_i})) }{\prod_{q=1}^s P[g(\mathbf{T}_{q,N_i}) = g(\mathbf{t}_{q,N_i}) | \mathbf{R}_{\bar{q}N_i}]}
\] where \(\mathbf{R}_{\bar{s}N_i}\) is the “history of \(\mathbf{R}_{sN_i}\)”. e.g.
\[
\mathbf{R}_{\bar{3}N_i} = [\mathbf{R}_{1N_i}, \mathbf{R}_{2N_i}, \mathbf{R}_{3N_i}]
\]


C.3.5 Notes

We have turned the bipartite graph situation into one which approcimates IID sampling.
Each observation comes with its own measures as well as the network exposure values
It is possible to fully ascertain the measures on included observations
It is possible to imagine a super-populaton consisting of individuals independently censored from the sample, but each with fully observed network exposure values since it is a bipartite network and since all places are fully ascertained.
In the next section we show how a model like this can be used to coordinate a real outbreak response whetehr it be vaccination or referral for screening, or intensified information.

title: C - SSNAC III: Causality
text:
C.4 Vaccine strategy model


We used data from RESPND-MI to assess the effectiveness of two approaches to conducting mass vaccination campaigns quickly. MPX NYC is an online survey of about 1300 individuals that was conducted in 2022 in New York City. Study participants were asked to indicate their home on a map and were asked to indicate places they had had social contact in a congregate setting. Spatial coordinates were converted into community district identifiers. Community districts spatially partition the city of New York.
Under the SSNAC framework, our intervention of interest might not be about setting the value of any particular variable, but setting a policy or a process that produces a set of variables in the causal model. This would be done by changing the structural equations which produce those variables. In the SWING shown in Figure C.15 and Equation C.16, we show an intervention which replaces the function for the risk rating for each community (\(\mathbf{R}\)) with the function \(h\). Every variable that is downstream of the first variable created using \(h\) is marked with a superscript \((h)\) to show that it is partially determined by that function.
We can now ask what the impact of taking policy \(h\) would be on the decision whether or not to vaccinate a neighborhood \(j\) at time \(s\) (\(T_{js}\)). We can also ask what the impact of the policy is on the the exposure of participant \(i\) to the campaign message at time \(s\) (\(M_{is}\)).
Our interest in RESPND-MI, however, was initially to provide evidence to inform a targeted vaccination campaign, so the main outcomes of interest are the vaccination status of each individual \(i\) at time \(s\) (\(V^{(h)}_{is}\)). We were interested in contrasting two approaches to assigning risk-ratings to community districts: the contact-neutralizing approach and the movement-neutralizing approach.
Whereas the contact-neutralizing approach ranks community districts by how many individuals are connected to them, the movement-neutralizing approach ranks community districts by how centrally they are connected to other community districts through the exchange of individuals.


C.4.1 Assumptions
We make the simplifying assumption that only one neighborhood is vaccinated at a time - the top-ranked one. We make the further simplifying assumptions that every person associated with a community district (either through residence or social activity) receives the campaign message when a community district is vaccinated, and that every person who receives a campaign message gets vaccinated. Once an individual is vaccinated, they remain vaccinated.


C.4.2 Structural equations
According to the model specified by structural equations C.16, no individual \(i\) has been vaccinated at time 0, and nobody receives the campaign message. The risk rating for community district \(j\) at time \(s\) is some function \(h\) of the vaccination status at time \(s-1\) for each individual who is connected to that community district. An intervention is conducted in community district \(j\) as time \(s\) if that community district has the highest risk rating. Each individual \(i\) is said to have received the campaign message at time \(s\) if the intervention was conducted in any of the community districts he is connected to. Finally, we consider individual \(i\) vaccinated at time \(s\) if they were vaccinated at time \(s-1\) or if they received the campaign message in time \(s\). The risk rating is given by the function \(h\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_{0i} &=  0 \\
V_{0i} &=  0 \\
R_{sj}^{(h)} &=  h(\mathbf{V}_{s-1}) \\
T_{sj}^{(h)} &=  \begin{cases} 1 & R_{sj}^{(h)} = max_k R_{sk}^{(h)} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
M_{si}^{(h)} &=  \begin{cases} 1 & \mathbf{T}_{s\mathscr{N}_i}^{(h)} \neq \mathbf{0}  \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
V_{si}^{(h)} &=  \begin{cases} 1 & M_{si}^{(h)} = 1 \text{ or } V_{s-1,i}^{(h)} = 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{C.16}\]

program_dang_mpx_nyc() |>
  plot_swig(node_radius = 0.5, nudge_intervention_labels = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_mpxnyc(option = "light") +
  scale_color_mpxnyc(option = "manual", values = c("Community" = "black", "Individual" = "black", "Graph" = "black")) +
  theme_mpxnyc_blank()








Figure C.15: SWING for Week 1-3 in RESPND-MI Application of SSNAC framework





Define \(\psi(i, j)\) as an adjacency function - an indicator function that equals to \(1\) if Person \(i\) lives in or visits neighborhood \(j\) and \(0\) otherwise. Let \(\mathscr{N}_P\) be the indices of all person nodes and \(\mathscr{N}_N\) be a set of indices for neighborhood nodes. Under the contact-neutralizing approach:
\[
h_{sj}(\mathbf{V}_{s-1}) = \sum_{ i \in \mathscr{N}_P} (1 -V_{(s-1), i}) \times \psi(i, j)   
\]
and under the movement-neutralizing approach:
\[
h_{sj}(\mathbf{V}_{s-1}) =   \sum_{ i \in \mathscr{N}_P} (1 -V_{(s-1), i}) \times \psi(i, j) \sum_{ k \in \mathscr{N}_N} \psi(i, k)
\]


C.4.3 Estimands

Spatial efficiency
Intervention coverage for the \(s^{th}\) community district to be immunized, is defined:
\[
C_s^{(h)} = \frac{1}{|\mathscr{N}_p|}\sum_i V_{si}^{(h)}
\]
The cumulative intervention coverage after immunizing \(s\) community districts is therefore:
\[
\bar{C_s}^{(h)} = \sum_{v = 1}^s{C_v }^{(h)}
\]


Social network impact
Define graph \(G^{s}(N, \psi_s)\) such that:
\[
\psi_s(i, j) = \psi(i, j) \times (1 -V_{(s-1), i})
\]
The cumulative social network impact of immunizing \(s\) community districts is measured in terms of the size of the largest of the connected components \(LCC_{(s)}\) of the \(G^{s}(N, \psi_s)\) network as a proportion of the total number of participants.
\[
\frac{LCC_s}{|N_p|}
\]



C.4.4 Estimation
We simulated the intervention outlined above using RESPND-MI data by calculating the \(G^{s}(N, \psi_s)\) where \(s\) ranges from \(1\) to the total number of community districts. We measured the uncertainty of our estimates by re-sampling study participants with replacement.

title: C - SSNAC III: Causality
text:
Notes

a. Definitions

Classic causal inference

Definition C.33 (Random variable) A random scalar quantity assumed to behave according some (unknown) probability distribution.


Definition C.34 (Statistical model) A collection of probability distributions \(\mathcal M\) on a vector of random variables \(\mathbf V\). Probability distributions in this model are characterized using a set of parameters \(\mathbf \theta\).
\[
\mathcal{M}=\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\quad\text{on set of random variables }\mathbf V.
\]


Definition C.35 (Non-parametric structural equation model [NPSEM]) A statistical model characterized by a set of deterministic functions called structural equations. Each structural equation \(f_V\) returns the value of a random variable \(V\) in the model. It is a function of the other random variables as well as a random error term \(U\):
\[
\theta =\{f_{V}(\mathbf V_{-V}, U_V):V\in\mathbf V\}.
\]
Where \(\mathbf V_{-V}\) denotes the sub-vector of \(\mathbf V\) that excludes \(V\). By definition, no random variable is directly or indirectly a function of itself, so we can order the random variables and write each as a function of prior random variables:
\[
V_{j} \;=\; f_{V_j}\!\big( V_{1},\dots,V_{j-1},\, U_{V_j} \big).
\]


Definition C.36 (NPSEM with independent errors [NPSEM-IE]) An NPSEM with mutually independent error terms.
\[
j\neq k  \iff  U_{V_j} \perp U_{V_k}
\]


Definition C.37 (Parent) A random variable \(X\) is a parent to random variable \(Y\) if \(X\) appears in the structural equation for \(Y\). The set of parents for \(X\) is denoted \(\mathbf{Pa}(X)\).


Definition C.38 (Observational unit) A sub-vector \(\mathscr{O}_i, i \in [1,n]\) of the random variables \(\mathbf V\) such that:
\[
\mathbf V = \big[ \mathscr{O}_1, ..., \mathscr{O}_n\big]^T
\]


Definition C.39 (Equivalence) Two random variables are equivalent if they belong to different observational units but represent the same construct.
\[
X_i\sim X_j\iff \ X_i\in  \mathscr{O}_i;\ X_j\in  \mathscr{O}_j,\ X_i \text{ same construct } X_j \ (i\ne j).
\]


Definition C.40 (No spillover assumption) The assumption that no variable is a parent of an equivalent variable in another observational unit.
\[
X\notin \mathbf{Pa}(X')\quad
\forall\, X\sim X',\ X\in \mathscr O_i,\ X'\in \mathscr O_j,\ i\ne j.
\]


Definition C.41 (No interference assumption) The assumption that no variable is a parent of a non-equivalent variable in another observational unit.
\[
X\notin \mathbf{Pa}(Y)\quad
\forall\, X\in \mathscr O_i,\ Y\in \mathscr O_j,\ X\not\sim Y \ i\ne j
\]


Definition C.42 (Identical distributions assumption) The assumption that equivalent variables have identical structural equations.
\[
X_i\sim X_j\Rightarrow f_{X_i}=f_{X_j}.
\]


Definition C.43 (Intervention equation) An intervention equation in relation to random variable \(V\) is a deterministic function \(h\) with the same inputs and outputs as the structural equation for \(V\).


Definition C.44 (Intervention regime) A set of intervention equations defined on a subset of random variables \(\mathbf E \subset \mathbf V\).
\[
\Gamma = \{ h_V \}_{V \in \mathbf{E}}
\]


Definition C.45 (Interventional NPSEM) An NPSEM \(\mathcal{M}\) for which a subset of structural equations \(\mathbf E\) have been replaced by intervention equations in intervention regime \(\Gamma\).
\[
\mathcal{M}^{(\Gamma)} =  \{f_V^{(\Gamma)}: V \in \mathbf V \}
\]
\[
f_V^{(\Gamma)} = \begin{cases}
  h_V & \text{if}  & V \in \mathbf E\\
  f_V & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]


Definition C.46 (Causal model) A causal model \(\mathcal C\) of “observational” NPSEM \(\mathcal M\) under intervention \(\Gamma\) is an NPSEM that is generated by combining \(\mathcal M\) with its interventional NPSEMs \(\mathcal M^{(\Gamma_1)}...\mathcal M^{(\Gamma_q)}\) and constraining the error term for each random variable in the interventional NPSEM equations so that it is equal to the error term for the same variable in the observational NPSEM.
\[
\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{M} \cup \mathcal M^{(\Gamma_1)} \cup ... \cup \mathcal M^{(\Gamma_q)}
\]
\[
\text{for all } V \in \mathbf V, \quad {U_V} = {U}^{(\Gamma_1)}_V = ... = {U}^{(\Gamma_q)}_V
\]


Definition C.47 (FFRCISTG model) A finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (FFRCISTG) is a causal model of an NPSEM-IE \(\mathcal M\) under intervention regime \(\Gamma\). By assumption, \(\mathcal M\) satisfies: (1) no spillover, (2) no interference, and (3) identical distributions.



Network causal inference

Definition C.48 (Graph) An ordered pair \(\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)\) with node set \(\mathcal{N}\)and adjacency function \(\psi\). The adjacecy function assigns a nonnegative weight to each unordered pair of nodes \((i,j)\).
\[
\mathscr G=(\mathcal N,\psi),\qquad
\psi:\mathcal N\times\mathcal N\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0},\qquad
\psi(i,j)=\psi(j,i)
\]
Nodes \(i,j \in \mathcal{N}\) are connected if and only if \(\psi(i,j) > 0\).


Definition C.49 (Neighborhood) The set of nodes connected to a given node \(i \in \mathcal{N}\) in graph \(\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)\).
\[
\mathcal{N}_i = \{ j \in \mathcal{N} : \psi(i,j) > 0 \}.
\]


Definition C.50 (Network weights) The vector representing the edges a given node \(i\) shares with other nodes in graph \(\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)\).
\[
\Psi_i = [\psi(i,1), \dots, \psi(i,n)]^T
\qquad n=|\mathcal N|.
\]


Definition C.51 (Network values) The sub-vector of some \(\mathbf X \in \{0,1\}^n\) that is related to nodes in the neighborhood of \(i\) in graph \(\mathscr{G} = (\mathcal{N}, \psi)\)
\[
\mathbf X_{\mathcal N_i}=\big(X_j\big)_{j\in \mathcal N_i}
\]


Definition C.52 (Exposure mapping) A function \(g_i : \{0,1\}^{K \times n} \to \mathbb{R}^m\)
such that
\[
Y_i = f_{Y_i}\big(g_i(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K), U_{Y_i}\big).
\]
where \(f_{Y_i}\) is the structural equation for \(Y_i\), and are each an equivalence class induced by the equivalence relation among the parents of \(Y\).


Definition C.53 (Separability) The assumption that an exposure mapping \(g_i\) can be written:
\[
g_i(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_K)
  = \big[ \begin{pmatrix} X_{1i} \\ \dots \\ X_{Ki} \end{pmatrix},\, g_{1i}(\mathbf{X}_1),\, \dots,\, g_{Ki}(\mathbf{X}_K)\big]^T,
\]
where \(X_{ki}\) is the \(i^{th}\) entry of \(\mathbf V_k\) and each \(g_{ti} : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is a component function of \(g_i\). A structural equation is said to be separable if its exposure mapping is separable.


Definition C.54 (Positional invariance) The assumption that the value of component function \(g_{ti}\) is invariant under a re-ordering of network values and an identical re-ordering of network weights. i.e. \(g_{ti}\) is positionally invariant with respect to \(\mathscr{G}_t\) if for all \(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{X}' \in \{0,1\}^n\)
\[
\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{X}'_{\mathcal{N}_j},
\quad
\Psi_{i,\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\Psi_{j,\mathcal{N}_j}
\Rightarrow
g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) = g_{tj}(\mathbf{X}').
\]
An exposure mapping shows positional invariance with respect to graph set \(\mathcal H = \{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}\) if it is separable and all its component functions show positional invariance with respect to an element of \(\{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}\). A structural equation is positionally invariant if its exposure mapping is positionally invariant.


Definition C.55 (Boundedness) The assumption that a component function \(g_{ti}\) can only take on values from a finite set. i.e. \(g_{ti}\) is bounded if there exists a finite set \(\mathcal{D}\) and a constant \(c\) such that for \(\mathbf{X} \in \{0,1\}^n\)
\[
g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) \in \mathcal{D} \quad \text{ for }|\mathcal{D}|< c \in \mathbb{Z}.
\]
An exposure mapping is bounded if it is separable and all its component functions are bounded.


Definition C.56 (Network exposure mapping) A component function \(g_{ti}\) which is bounded and positionally invariant with respect to some graph \(\mathscr{G}_t\).


Definition C.57 (Homogeneous network interference) The assumption that an exposure mapping \(g_{ti}\) is separable and all its component functions are network exposure mappings with respect to some graph set \(\mathcal H\). An NPSEM satisfies homogenous network interference if all its exposure mappings satisfy homogenous network interference.


Definition C.58 (NFFRCISTG model) A network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (NFFRCISTG) is a causal model of an NPSEM-IE \(\mathcal M\) under intervention regime \(\Gamma\). By assumption, \(\mathcal M\) satisfies: (1) no spillover, (2) homogenous network interference with respect to some graph set \(\mathcal H\), and (3) identical distributions.



Social and spatial inference

Definition C.59 (Graph generator) An \(n \times n\) array of structural equations which collectively model the edges of a random graph.
An \(n \times n\) function \([f_{\psi_{ij}}]_{i,j \in \mathcal N}\) whose entries \(\psi(i,j)\) are each a deterministic symmetric function of the other variables in the model along with an error term.
\[
\psi(i,j) = f_{\psi_{ij}}(\mathbf{Pa}(\psi(i,j)), U_{\psi_{ij}})
\]
such that
\[
U_{\psi_{ij}} = U_{\psi_{ji}} \text{ and } f_{\psi_{ij}} = f_{\psi_{ji}}
\]


Definition C.60 (NPSEM-NE) An NPSEM with networked errors is an NPSEM which includes random graph generators among the structural equations. Error terms are correlated within each graph generator but independent across graph generators, between structural equations and graph generators, and between structural equations.


Definition C.61 (Homogenous random network interference) An exposure mapping exhibits homogeneous random network interference with respect to a random graph set \(\{\psi_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}\) if it is separable and all its component functions are network exposure mappings. An NPSEM exhibiits homogenous random network interference if all its exposure mappings exhibit homogenous randomn network interference.


Definition C.62 (RNFFRCISTG) A random network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (RNFFRCISTG) model is a causal model defined on a random graph NPSEM-NE which satisfies the (1) no spillover, (2) homogenous random network interference with respect to random graph set \(\mathcal H \subset \mathbf V\), and (3) identical distributions assumptions.


Definition C.63 (Bipartite NPSEM-IE) A random bipartite graph NPSEM-IE is a random graph NPSEM which whose generators produce bipartite graphs on the same partitioning of \(\mathbf V\).


Definition C.64 (BRNFFRCISTG model) A bipartite random network finest fully randomized causally interpretable structured tree graph (BRNFFRCISTG) model is a causal model defined on a bipartite random graph NPSEM-IE which satisfies the (1) no spillover, (2) homogenous random network interference, and (3) identical distributions assumptions.




b. Boundedness
The assumption of boundedness can obtain in three different ways. It could be as a result of restrictions on the structure of the graph. For example, if the only relationships of interest between individual participants were marriages, each node would have a degree of either 0 or 1, meaning the count of alters with \(X_{tj} = 1, j \in \mathscr{N}_i\) is either zero or one.
It might obtain via restrictions on the value of \(\mathbf{X}\) itself. It might be the case, for instance, that the count of \(i\)’s for which \(X_{ti}=1\) is very low so that on average, the count of alters for which \(X_{tj} = 1, j \in N_i\) will also be low.
Finally, boundedness could obtain as a result of the functional form of \(g\) itself. This might happen if \(g\) models a network exposure which has a ceiling effect in its dose-response curve with the outcome of interest. For example, if \(X\) indicates ownership of a car, and \(\mathscr{G}\) encodes close friendships, \(g\) would be a network exposure mapping which tells us how each additional friend who has a car shifts the outcome of interest. For most health applications, its likely that beyond some number of friends who have a car, an additional friend who gets a car will not change the outcome.


c. D-separation
D-separation is a set of rules for translating DAGs into conditional independence statements. A pair of nodes is d-separated if all the paths linking them are closed or if there is no path that links them. A pair of nodes is conditionally d-separated if all the paths linking them are closed after conditioning on some set of nodes.
A path is a sequence of nodes that starts with an origin node and ends with a terminal node. Consecutive entries in the sequence are connected in the DAG. A path of length one is open by definition. A path of length two or more is open if all its triangles are open.
A triangle is a sub-sequence of a path which contains three consecutive nodes from the path. A canonical triangle is one in which we do not condition on the apex node. A conditional triangle is one in which we do condition.

D.1 Person–Place Network Mapper
We designed, tested, and implemented the MPX NYC Person–Place Network Mapper to address practical and ethical challenges in collecting sensitive spatial data in an anonymous survey. Our aim was to capture information on venues participants visited, including those where group sex occurred, while minimizing the risk of re-identification through location data.

title: D - SSNAC IV: Measurement
text:
D.1.1 Place Mapping
Because participants were unlikely to recall precise addresses or zip codes, we used the Google Maps API to let them identify locations by landmarks, cross-streets, subway stations, and neighborhood names. The map displayed detailed geographic information with standard navigation tools (see Figure D.1).
Participants were prompted to identify specific types of places, such as their primary residence, and then to select additional locations where they had physical or sexual contact in group settings. Each tap on the map placed a marker, which triggered follow-up questions about activity at that site and the type of venue.






Figure D.1: Map input question format developed for MPX NYC





D.1.2 Link Tracing
We developed a referral system to build a network anonymously. At the start of the survey, participants received a unique identifier card containing a QR code and word combination, which they were asked to save.
At the end of the survey, participants could share a pre-written invitation with a unique URL. If a contact used the link, an edge was added between the two respondents in the graph database. When a new participant connected with someone who had already completed the survey, the existing participant could confirm their identifier card, allowing the system to link their nodes without revealing identities.



Surey share dialogue




D.1.3 Implementation
To reduce re-identification risk, spatial data were coarsened before storage. For example, coordinates were converted to census tract identifiers, preventing disclosure of exact locations such as a dormitory or government office.
The tool’s front end was built as a single-page React/NextJS application hosted on Vercel, with design based on the MPX NYC style guide. The back end used a custom Neo4j graph database. Standard survey formats (multiple choice, text, etc.) were integrated alongside the mapping and referral components.
Data flow proceeded as follows: the front end loaded questions from a JSON file, parsed referral identifiers and language settings from the URL, and requested a public identifier from the API. The API generated and stored public/private identifier pairs in a secure table, returned the public identifier and QR code to the participant, and transformed identifiers before sending responses to the graph database.
For spatial inputs, the front end queried the FCC API, which returned census block identifiers. These were truncated to census tract identifiers before being stored in the study database. Two rounds of user testing with about ten participants each informed refinements to usability and clarity.

Principles
The success of the RESPND-MI study was grounded in a set of deeply held principles that guided every aspect of its formation and operation. At its core was a commitment to community empowerment—the belief that queer and trans communities possess the expertise and insight needed to understand and address their own health challenges. Rather than treating community members as informants or subjects, the study positioned them as co-investigators and decision-makers, capable of shaping research design, communication strategies, and interpretation of findings. This approach drew inspiration from Global South frameworks of health activism that emphasize sex positivity, mutual trust, and community ownership of knowledge. Transparency and accountability were essential: data were collected and used first and foremost to serve the community, rather than to fulfill institutional mandates.
The group also operated on a set of internal principles that sustained its collaborative energy during the emergency. Participation was designed to bring joy rather than stress, ensuring that contributors felt energized by their involvement. The organizing culture embraced experimentation and low-stakes failure, recognizing that in moments of crisis, iteration and imperfection are essential to learning. The group’s ethos of “abundance and redundancy” valued overlapping initiatives as sources of resilience rather than inefficiency. A commitment to democracy ensured that decisions were made collectively and transparently, while the principle of “building as we fly” allowed for adaptability in rapidly changing conditions. Finally, the team maintained a constant awareness of power and history. By explicitly situating their work within a decolonial critique of global health, the investigators sought to reverse the traditional direction of knowledge transfer—from the Global South to the Global North—and to demonstrate that community-led monitoring and accountability could strengthen, rather than oppose, scientific rigor.


Practices
RESPND-MI translated these principles into practice through participatory co-design, distributed leadership, iterative, task-oriented collaboration, and a tight project management system that balanced autonomy with accountability. The LGBTQ+ Community Forum (CF), launched in May 2022, became the centerpiece of this participatory infrastructure. Initially conceived as a space for consultation, the CF rapidly evolved into a coordination mechanism that brought together activists, community leaders, public-health professionals, and researchers for weekly meetings. Over the course of the mpox emergency, more than eighty participants contributed to discussions and decisions that directly shaped the study. Forum members proposed the translation of the survey and outreach materials into Spanish, advised on the inclusion of transgender participants and iconography, selected outreach sites such as the Fire Island ferry terminal and LinkNYC kiosks, and helped refine messaging to avoid stigma. Through these interactions, the CF not only informed the research but also modeled a new form of shared governance that blurred the line between community organizing and epidemiologic investigation.
Internally, RESPND-MI’s tight project management system combined structure and flexibility. Teams worked from shared task lists that clarified responsibilities, timelines, and dependencies. Each participant tracked the status of their own work, marking tasks as complete or pending and reassigning them when necessary. This approach created clear lines of accountability without constraining creativity. Weekly investigator meetings served as synchronization points where team members reviewed feedback from the Community Forum, coordinated cross-functional work, and maintained momentum. These meetings also preserved space for informal connection and reflection—key ingredients for trust and sustained collaboration under crisis conditions.
RESPND-MI operated through distributed leadership rather than hierarchy. Authority was shared across functional leads who coordinated distinct domains of work while remaining accountable to the collective. The Principal Investigator anchored the overall vision and ethical integrity of the project, while the Research Coordinator maintained its rhythm and logistics. The Communications Lead shaped external messaging, the Questionnaire and Translation Leads ensured inclusivity and linguistic accessibility, and the Web Development Lead managed the group’s digital infrastructure. This networked form of leadership ensured that decisions were informed by diverse expertise, that no single bottleneck slowed the process, and that community voices remained central to every stage of design and implementation.
The organizing culture emphasized making things quickly and collectively. Rather than waiting for perfect consensus, teams prioritized the rapid production of useful outputs—policy briefs, educational materials, safer-sex guidance, vaccination locators, and op-eds—that directly met community needs in real time. The group’s motto—“talk to people and make things”—captured its pragmatic rhythm: ongoing dialogue with communities fed directly into the creation of tangible tools, which in turn generated new conversations and collaborations. Dissemination was integral to this practice, not a postscript. The team engaged with press outlets, government partners, and academic audiences to amplify community expertise as public-health expertise, presenting at venues ranging from ballroom community events to the World Health Organization and the International AIDS Society.


Structures
Beneath these principles and practices lay a set of organizational structures that made coordination possible. The investigator group organized its work around four core functions: coordination, surveillance, health communication, and resourcing. Coordination focused on gathering and sharing information among stakeholders, documenting the experiences of community-based organizations, and aligning programmatic activities across sectors. Surveillance addressed the group’s data needs—identifying gaps, synthesizing information, and making data accessible to both stakeholders and the public. Health communication combined the development of new materials with amplification of messages generated within communities themselves. Resourcing sustained the other three functions by identifying and mobilizing support from queer-serving companies, donors, foundations, and public agencies.
Together, these functions formed a dynamic ecosystem in which the Community Forum and the Investigator Group worked in tandem. The forum served as an open, participatory sphere for discussion and collective decision-making, while the investigator group translated that input into operational and scientific outputs. The arrangement allowed RESPND-MI to act both as a research project and as a coordination platform for community response. This structure enabled speed without sacrificing inclusivity or rigor: decisions were made collectively, outputs were produced iteratively, and community feedback remained at the center of every process.
The project’s dissemination network extended across scales. Locally, the team collaborated with the New York City Department of Health, community-based organizations, and cultural networks such as ballroom houses. Nationally, it contributed to advocacy initiatives like the Choice Agenda and AVAC’s panels on mpox and HIV activism. Internationally, the study was presented as a model of rapid, community-led response at venues including the WHO and the International AIDS Society. Through these efforts, RESPND-MI demonstrated that a decentralized, joyful, and accountable public-health research collective could operate as effectively—and often more equitably—than traditional institutions.


Conclusion
In sum, the RESPND-MI study succeeded because it wove together a coherent set of principles, practices, and structures that mutually reinforced one another. Its guiding principles—community empowerment, joy and democracy in participation, accountability, and decolonization—defined a moral and epistemic stance. Its participatory and distributed practices turned those ideals into action through co-design, shared leadership, iterative making, and disciplined project management. Its organizational structures provided the scaffolding that allowed those practices to scale and sustain themselves under the pressure of a public-health emergency. The result was a form of community-led epidemiologic inquiry that not only generated data but transformed the conditions under which data are produced, shared, and acted upon. RESPND-MI stands as evidence that community power, when structured intentionally and supported with care, can yield both scientific insight and collective liberation.

To maximize the speed of recruitment, we invested in a bilingual, culturally competent communication campaign in collaboration with a marketing agency. The brief was to create a name and marketing concept that convey scientific rigor, build trust with the community, and stand out in a crowded online marketplace (see ?fig-requirements). As a starting point, the RESPND-MI team suggested a campaign that playfully uses emojis that have sexual connotations in queer and trans communities, and that integrates LGBT social media influencers as a communication channel.



Requirements for MPX NYC Study


The RESPND-MI study team approached marketing not as a top-down broadcast but as a community-driven endeavor. From the very beginning, we partnered closely with the RESPND-MI LGBTQ+ Community Forum (CF) to workshop language, imagery, and channel preferences. We partnered with a marketing agency to, asking them to name the campaing and provide a marketing concept. Two campaign names and four marketing concepts (see Figure G.1) were developed by the marketing agency and presented to a meeting of the CF. The final concept and name were decided by consensus during that meeting.
Focus-group feedback shaped both the voice and visual style of our materials, ensuring they read not like clinical advisories but as messages “of us, by us.” This co-creation process helped us land on the right balance of urgency and relatability and guided decisions about everything from color palettes to tone, emoji use, and even the inclusion of playful vernacular.
We developed a suite of branded assets in a social media toolkit: digital graphics, animated GIFs, flyers, and social-media posts. These assets used vibrant hues, harm-reduction tips, and emojis — symbols that queer and trans people often use to communicate about sex — to frame health education and participation in the survey as both essential and empowering.
To maximize reach and resonance, we layered in both influencer amplification and strategically targeted placements. Short, scripted mpox-education videos were produced on Cameo by celebrity personalities familiar to queer audiences—ranging from reality-TV stars to drag queens to Broadway actors. We distributed the videos on social media on the RESPND-MI website and newsletter. Concurrently, we secured out-of-home placements on high-foot-traffic venues (such as Fire Island ferry terminals and LinkNYC kiosks) and in-app slots on Grindr, a popular dating platform. Notably, Grindr provided the RESPND-MI study team with pro bono ad space to recruit participants. Because New York’s queer and trans communities are linguistically diverse, every piece of collateral was produced in both English and Spanish.
In addition, we placed “Six Ways We Can Have Safer Sex in the Time of Monkeypox,” a list of harm-reduction tips, in POZ Magazine. With support from UCLA Luskin School of Public Affairs, we translated those six harm-reduction tips into graphics for social media. Mass media, such as The Los Angeles Times and Last Week Tonight with John Oliver, amplified the harm-reduction tips in their publications, further extending our reach.
By combining community-led design, professional creative execution, influencer storytelling, targeted media buys, and bilingual harm-reduction messaging, the RESPND-MI marketing approach exemplified how culturally attuned public health communication can drive both engagement and impact.
